To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

angiotensine II (AII), a hormone that plays a major role in blood pressure regulation, binds to liver membranes and that the binding of AII to liver membranes can be affected by dietary sodium intake.

1) Angiotensin II receptor density and affinity are regulated by dietary Na+ intake; 2) Angiotensins II and III are the major circulating forms of angiotensin in rats fed a low Na+ diet; 3) The liver is a site of angiotensins II, III, and IV metabolism; and 4) Angiotensinin II and angiotensins III and IV may have different functions in the liver.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the renin angiotensin system (RAS), and in particular the role of angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) in the regulation of the RAS in the rat.
the regulation of hepatic angiotensin receptors by dietary Na+ or by angiotensin itself.
the study of the binding of angiotensin analogues to the rat liver and the effect of Na intake on this binding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver has a high affinity binding site that has the characteristics of an AII receptor.
angiotensins are not only involved in the control of blood pressure but also in the regulation of liver function.
the liver has specific receptors for AII which are regulated by dietary Na+ in a manner which is consistent with a physiological role in the control of Na+ balance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver has a receptor for angiotensin, that it is similar to the vascular type 2 receptor and that it is regulated by Na+ intake.
the liver angiotensin receptors are regulated by dietary Na+ intake.

the liver AII receptor has the characteristics of an AII receptor, that it is regulated by dietary Na+ in a biphasically manner, that the biphasic response is due to a combination of receptor up-regulation and down-regulation, and that the biphasically response is not due to the presence of a second type of AII receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver has a specific receptor for angiotensin, which is regulated by dietary salt.
the angiotensin receptor is a good target for drug therapy in liver disease.
there is a significant difference in the binding of AII to the liver and kidney.
